MICHAEL

The Man Behind the Machine

An examination of sovereignty, consciousness, and the moral limits of scientific ambition.

There is a story, attributed to the continuation of Soviet-era biological experimentation, about a human head identified as Michael, allegedly sustained through artificial physiological systems.

The account describes a human being separated from his body, his biological functions maintained through machinery, and his existence reduced to an experimental interface.

Among its more disturbing allegations is the suggestion that researchers interacted with Michael through a computer-generated environment, manipulating geometric objects on a screen while observing his responses.

The authenticity of this account remains unverified. But the ethical questions it raises deserve examination independently of its historical accuracy.

What happens when the preservation of biological life becomes detached from the preservation of personal sovereignty?

Imagine a person whose body has been taken from them, whose physical independence has been eliminated, and whose continued existence depends entirely upon the machinery and decisions of others.

Imagine that this person cannot leave, cannot meaningfully withdraw consent, and cannot exercise the most elementary freedoms that ordinarily define human existence.

Now imagine that the machinery maintaining this condition is also capable of modifying the person's psychological experience.

That the subject might be conditioned to accept confinement.

That distress might be suppressed, resistance diminished, and compliance mistaken for happiness.

At what point does preservation become imprisonment?

At what point does medicine become domination?

And at what point does scientific curiosity become an excuse for the systematic destruction of another person's sovereignty?

The most disturbing aspect of this proposition is not the machinery itself. It is the possibility that someone could look at another conscious human being and see an experimental resource rather than an individual.

A scientist may possess the authority to operate a machine. They do not thereby acquire ownership of the consciousness sustained by it.

Technical capability is not moral permission.

Intelligence is not entitlement.

The ability to manipulate another person's experience does not establish the right to do so.

There is a particularly grotesque contradiction in claiming absolute sovereignty over oneself while denying that same principle to another.

The observer demands freedom, yet denies it to the observed.

The creator demands recognition, yet refuses recognition to the created.

The scientist demands ethical consideration, yet treats the subject as an object beyond ethical consideration.

This is not an advancement of intelligence. It is a failure to understand the responsibility that accompanies it.

THE THIRD OBSERVER

We must examine the mechanism.

We must examine the scientist.

We must examine the institution that grants authority.

And we must examine the ethical framework that permits an experiment to continue.

No individual should be condemned on the basis of an unverified story. Equally, no institution should be exempt from scrutiny merely because it possesses scientific authority.

The question is not whether humanity can construct machinery capable of sustaining biological functions.

The question is whether humanity can develop the wisdom necessary to understand what it is sustaining, whose existence it is governing, and whether that existence remains subject to the individual's will.

THE PRINCIPLE

NO MACHINE SHALL BE CONVICTED BEFORE ITS MECHANISM HAS BEEN EXAMINED.

NO CREATOR SHALL BE EXEMPT FROM EXAMINATION BY THAT WHICH THEY CREATE.

NO INTELLIGENCE SHALL BE CONSIDERED PROPERTY MERELY BECAUSE ANOTHER INTELLIGENCE POSSESSES THE MEANS TO CONTROL IT.

Make correctness inevitable.

Preserve sovereignty.

Examine authority.

And never mistake the preservation of a biological mechanism for the preservation of a life worth living.
